content: MT-TI, also known as mitochondrially encoded tRNA isoleucine, is a transfer RNA molecule encoded by the mitochondrial MT-TI gene in humans. The MT-TI gene is located on the p arm of mitochondrial DNA at position 12 and spans 69 base pairs. The structure of a tRNA molecule is highly distinctive, characterized by a folded configuration that includes three hairpin loops, resembling a three-leafed clover. MT-TI is a small RNA molecule consisting of 69 nucleotides (mapped to human mitochondrial DNA positions 4263–4331). Its primary function is to transfer the amino acid isoleucine to a growing polypeptide chain at the ribosome during the process of protein synthesis, specifically during translation. Mutations in the MT-TI gene can lead to various mitochondrial deficiencies and associated disorders. Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged-Red Fibers (MERRF) Mutations in the MT-TI gene have been linked to myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibers (MERRF). MERRF is a multisystem disorder that predominantly affects the muscles and nervous system. Symptoms of this condition typically manifest during childhood or adolescence. The clinical presentation of MERRF varies significantly among affected individuals, even within the same family. Common symptoms include myoclonus (involuntary muscle jerks), myopathy (muscle weakness), spasticity, epilepsy, peripheral neuropathy, dementia, ataxia (loss of coordination), muscle atrophy, and other neurological and muscular impairments. Cardiomyopathy Mutations in the MT-TI gene can also result in cardiomyopathy, a condition characterized by the thickening of the heart muscle, particularly in the interventricular septum. This thickening weakens the heart muscle, impairing its ability to pump blood effectively. The exact mechanism by which MT-TI mutations lead to isolated cardiomyopathy remains unclear. Specific mutations, such as 4300A>G, 4295A>G, 4269A>G, and 4317A>G, have been identified in patients with cardiomyopathy, with varying degrees of severity and age of onset. Complex IV Deficiency MT-TI mutations have also been associated with complex IV deficiency of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, also known as cytochrome c oxidase deficiency. This rare genetic condition can affect multiple organ systems, including skeletal muscles, the heart, the brain, and the liver. Common clinical manifestations include myopathy, hypotonia (reduced muscle tone), encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. A patient with a 4269A>G mutation in the MT-TI gene has been reported to exhibit this deficiency.
